articles.text: Piedmont City Administrator Sara Lillevand has announced she intends to retire in April next year, 2023. Lillevand has served as City Administrator since June 2019, when she was named to succeed former City Administrator Paul Benoit from a pool of over 40 applicants. Prior to becoming City Administrator she was the city’s Recreation Director for five years, from 2015 to 2019. Her earlier professional experience was as Athletic Director at Hayward State, as a collegiate basketball coach and kinesiology instructor. “I deeply appreciate the community of Piedmont. It is a special place with engaged residents and a genuinely committed, supportive, and indefatigable City Council. The staff are professional, dedicated, and caring; they respect each other and work as a team for the good of the community,” said Lillevand, a Piedmont native. “I am honored to have served as Recreation Director and City Administrator and will be forever grateful for both opportunities.” The city has benefited from Lillevand’s leadership since her appointment four years ago, Mayor Teddy Gray King said. “Throughout her time in Piedmont, she has put the community first. Since becoming City Administrator, Sara has deftly guided the City through the COVID-19 pandemic, and the uncertainties and changes that this time brought. She worked tirelessly to bring the Piedmont Community Pool project to fruition, through the design phase, and soon to construction. Sara’s efforts to maintain high service levels, excellent public facilities, and make Piedmont a better place for its residents will not soon be forgotten,” said Mayor King. “We will all miss her professional leadership and optimistic outlook and I will personally miss her guidance and friendship.” Lillevand will remain in her position until April 5, 2023 or until the position is filled, whichever is earlier. Recruitment for her replacement will begin immediately, the city confirmed. Piedmont City Administrator has announced her plans to retire next spring.

articles.text: Piedmont will hold its general municipal election on November 8. Three City Council seats and two School Board seats will be on the ballot. Seven residents have obtained nomination papers as of August 1 for city council, and three have obtained papers for School Board. One resident, Avnish Patel, has obtained nomination papers for both City Council and School Board. There are no Incumbent school board members running for re-election. City Council incumbents Betsy Andersen and Jennifer Long, and candidates Tom Ramsey, Bridget Harris, Avnish Patel, Jeanne Solnordal, and Nancy Bostrom also have obtained nomination papers for City Council. Ruchi Medhekar, Lindsay Thomasson obtained nomination papers for School Board. City council members Andersen and Long are eligible to run for an additional four-year term. Long was appointed in February and is currently serving in an interim role. She was appointed to the position by City Council following former vice mayor Tim Rood’s resignation in December 2021. Mayor Teddy Gray King is completing eight years on Council and is not eligible to run again. Former school board member Megan Pillsbury was eligible to run for an additional four-year term but moved out of town and is no longer eligible. Incumbent Amal Smith has termed out. The nomination period closes this Friday, August 12, at 5 p.m. If an eligible incumbent does not file nomination papers by August 12, the filing period for that office will be extended to August 17. articles.text: Because I love baseball, I preach an annual baseball-themed sermon This is the 2022 edition of my expression of love for the game. I love baseball. I love it because it fills me with many happy childhood memories. I love it because the goal of the game is to return home. I love it because a game proceeds at its own pace; it isn’t completely bound to a timeclock. I love it because, as a game in which failure abounds (the best hitters fail in their task seven out of ten times), it is a game I can relate to. I love it because it is a game of beautiful voices, among them Vin Scully, voice of the Los Angeles Dodgers from 1950- 2016. Vin died last week and I join with the millions of others who mourn his passing. In recent years my love for the game has taken the form of umpiring youth baseball games. Undeniably, my love for the game surpasses my skill as an officiant, but I try to do a credible job of helping young people and their families have a positive experience through the game of baseball. Every time I am on the diamond, I try to remember to take a deep breath and tell myself “It is a gift to be here.” Last fall, as part of a training series for umpires, we were taught that it would help us in our work if we remembered the letters E, L and M. • E for Effort. • L for Learning. Of the city’s four principal tennis courts, the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Vista and Bonita Avenues is the only one with lights. Throughout the week residents can play tennis until 9 p.m. Installation of six new light standards and double light fixtures was performed by Oakland based Gil’s Electric, the same company that some years ago installed the necklace of lights encircling Lake Merritt. The total cost for the four courts in Piedmont was $69,800 according to Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. The project included four new single-light fixtures, and new lighting controls with a digital time switch. “The new lights are designed to provide improved court illumination while reducing the offsite glare. articles.text: When Piedmont’s Housing Element requirement was initially announced, the Piedmont Planning staff informed residents that, even though the requirement of 587 units was nearly 10 times the previous requirement, “Piedmont should take on accommodating 587 units as a challenge.” There was no mention of challenging the 587-unit number, despite the drastic increase from the previous General Plan. Why challenge the State HCD (Housing and Community Development Dept.) requirement? One reason is that the State Auditor was directed to evaluate the needs assessment process that the HCD uses to provide key housing guidance to local governments. The Auditor’s report, dated March 17,2022, concluded that the HCD does not ensure that its needs assessments are accurate and adequately supported. The HCD response to this very serious finding was that it would review their processes over the next year, but they would not commit to reviewing or modifying any of the current cycle of projections. The State Auditor’s findings and conclusions introduce enough uncertainty about HCD requirements to warrant a serious inquiry or as some other like-minded cities have done – that is to band together and legally challenge the HCD on their process and projections. It is very important to remember that the General Plan will need to be resubmitted in 2031 and that the State will surely impose another housing requirement on Piedmont then. How many units and where will those units go? What legacy will be left for the City Council of 2031? It is very important that we and other cities push back and demand more transparency and accuracy from the HCD now. Another reason – our Fair Share. In the Aug. 1 Council meeting, many residents stated their belief that Piedmont should provide its fair share of housing units. I wholeheartedly agree but I also believe that our fair share should be derived from a fair and open process and that there should be some recognition of Piedmont’s constraints – that it is predominately built-out and that the City faces reconstruction or new construction of its Essential Services Buildings which could significantly affect some of the few available parcels in the City. Another reason – numbers matter. Many of the objections to the Housing Element come down to the extraordinary means needed to accommodate 587 units. If, for example, Piedmont’s Housing Element were only a 3-fold increase over the existing requirement and Piedmont needed to accommodate 180 units, I believe that the Housing Element would now be approved and in our rear-view mirror. Numbers do matter and accuracy and fairness of process matter. That is why I strongly urge the City Council to listen to the residents and take on the challenge – to investigate, question, and push back against the HCD 587-unit requirement and demand a fair process. –Donald Chandler, AIA “Things are looking better. Slow-paying customers are replacing non-pay customers.”
articles.title: Piedmont’s housing mandate needs to be challenged

Throughout the week residents can play tennis until 9 p.m. Installation of six new light standards and double light fixtures was performed by Oakland based Gil’s Electric, the same company that some years ago installed the necklace of lights encircling Lake Merritt. The total cost for the four courts in Piedmont was $69,800 according to Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. The project included four new single-light fixtures, and new lighting controls with a digital time switch. “The new lights are designed to provide improved court illumination while reducing the offsite glare. They should be a huge improvement over the previous configuration and provide the school and Recreation Department with the facilities that they need for their programming needs,” Gonzales said. Why challenge the State HCD (Housing and Community Development Dept.) requirement? One reason is that the State Auditor was directed to evaluate the needs assessment process that the HCD uses to provide key housing guidance to local governments. The Auditor’s report, dated March 17,2022, concluded that the HCD does not ensure that its needs assessments are accurate and adequately supported. The HCD response to this very serious finding was that it would review their processes over the next year, but they would not commit to reviewing or modifying any of the current cycle of projections. The State Auditor’s findings and conclusions introduce enough uncertainty about HCD requirements to warrant a serious inquiry or as some other like-minded cities have done – that is to band together and legally challenge the HCD on their process and projections. It is very important to remember that the General Plan will need to be resubmitted in 2031 and that the State will surely impose another housing requirement on Piedmont then. How many units and where will those units go? What legacy will be left for the City Council of 2031? It is very important that we and other cities push back and demand more transparency and accuracy from the HCD now. Another reason – our Fair Share. In the Aug. 1 Council meeting, many residents stated their belief that Piedmont should provide its fair share of housing units. I wholeheartedly agree but I also believe that our fair share should be derived from a fair and open process and that there should be some recognition of Piedmont’s constraints – that it is predominately built-out and that the City faces reconstruction or new construction of its Essential Services Buildings which could significantly affect some of the few available parcels in the City. Another reason – numbers matter. Many of the objections to the Housing Element come down to the extraordinary means needed to accommodate 587 units. If, for example, Piedmont’s Housing Element were only a 3-fold increase over the existing requirement and Piedmont needed to accommodate 180 units, I believe that the Housing Element would now be approved and in our rear-view mirror. Numbers do matter and accuracy and fairness of process matter. That is why I strongly urge the City Council to listen to the residents and take on the challenge – to investigate, question, and push back against the HCD 587-unit requirement and demand a fair process. –Donald Chandler, AIA READ IT IN THE POST “Things are looking better. articles.text: The Piedmont Community Band, led by majorette Elaine Lindenmayer, marches down Highland Avenue during the 4th of July parade, its only public appearance during the year. Part 2 of two-part series Piedmont Community Band members met on July 2 on Dracena Avenue for their only rehearsal of the year. Two days later they marched down Highland Avenue as a major participant in the city’s 4th of July Parade, their only public performance of the year. Mobilizing the band two days before the parade can be complicated, but this year With only about 30 musicians, ranging from amateur to professional, it was smooth sailing. Most musicians live in town, and some have been marching and playing with the band for well over 20 years. One family of musicians arrives from Minnesota as part of a family reunion. “This year, we did an [open call] for musicians. It can be hard to pin down volunteers who can perform in the parade and be there for rehearsal on July 2, so I’m always pleased by the level of participation,” band founder Jane Reed explained. The band includes musicians playing everything from trombone, trumpet, tuba, saxophone, clarinet, flute, to drums and even cymbals and a glockenspiel. “We sort of take whatever we can get,” Reed said with a smile. “We had a saxophone player’s wife play the cymbals this year.” The tradition of a one-rehearsal show has worked seamlessly, in part because the band plays the same three marches every year. The principal song is “On, Wisconsin!”, the high school standard. It is also an ode to Reed’s home-state of Wisconsin, where she learned to play The Piedmont Community Band near Piedmont Park. the alto saxophone growing up in high school. The band was led for a half dozen years by Ray Perman, a longtime percussionist in the band. He arranged for new neckerchiefs and caps for band members and was the first to connect all band members by e-mail and send music to everyone in advance. Resident Elaine Lindenmayer has led the band as majorette for 35 years. She first picked up a baton in high school and has twirled on and off throughout her life. In 1984, shortly after she moved to Piedmont, she heard the band practicing in front of her house on Highland Avenue. “When I heard them, I just wanted to march and twirl. I just have that percussion in my blood,” she said. Lindenmayer has held the baton since joining the band in its inception - taking off one year to give birth to son Evan in 1985. “I keep doing it because I have so much fun. Everyone lines up in front of my house year after year to rehearse (on July 4), and I know I could not sit in this house, hear that band, and not participate,” she said. Unlike playing from sheet music, Lindemayer’s routine changes each year. She said she tends to modify it during the parade. Her solo act – and the fact that she has been with the band since its very early days – gives her the creative liberty to explore different steps and twirls. Despite the absence of the city’s parade for two years due to COVID, the parade drew a large crowd this year. Lindenmayer said she noticed chairs lining the route as early as two weeks before July 4. The band picked up right where they left off in 2019. Reed credits the smooth sailing to the band members’ resilience and to its leader, Ken Kawaichi, who has led the band dressed as Emperor Norton for 36 years. The nod to Joshua Abraham Norton, who proclaimed himself “Norton, Emperor of the United States,” was joke that eventually became tradition - but added that Kawaichi, a skilled musician in his own right, leads the band every year with the same zeal. Photo by Ken DeCrosta Ken Kawaichi, dressed as Emperor Norton, leads the Piedmont Community Band in 2007 when it had more than 80 musicians.

articles.text: School will start slightly later for high school students this year, with classes beginning at 8:30 a.m., a half hour later than in prior years. The change is due to Senate Bill 328 approved by Governor Newsom on October 13, 2019. It applies to all high schools in the state. The last classes of the day will end at 3:25 p.m. on Mondays, and 3:35 p.m. on Tuesday and Thursdays. Classes will end at 2:50 p.m. on Wednesdays and Fridays. Piedmont High School conducted a pilot program for four weeks in January and February. During that time an additional period for office hours twice a week at the end of the day was tested and considered. It was learned that some upperclassmen with free 6th and 7th periods were asked to return to campus even after their last period. The additional periods are rescheduled this year to after brunch on Wednesday and Friday and will be called “Academy.” “There will certainly be a learning curve to start, but having gone through the pilot program last spring, we believe students and staff will grow into the new schedule quickly and take full advantage of its opportunities,” said school district Director of Communications Brian Killgore. The new state law also requires middle schools to start no earlier than 8:00 a.m. So while there was no requirement to change from the previous 8:20 a.m. start PMS did adjust its bell schedule on its own accord by moving the start time back to 8:40 a.m. Middle school will let out at a varying times throughout the week: Monday 3:24 p.m. Tuesday 3:08 p.m. Wednesday 2:41 p.m. Thursday 3:08 p.m. Friday 2:41 p.m. “Research shows that teenagers need more time to sleep at night for their well-being,” said PHS Principal Sukanya Goswami. “The benefit is for students to be in better spirits and well-rested when arriving on campus. This will not only help their mental well-being, but also with their academics,” she added. The school district said it will conduct evaluations throughout the school year and gather feedback from students, staff and families. A Bell Schedule Committee will reconvene in January for discussions and to plan for any adjustments for next year. articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District sent a letter to the school community authored by interim Superintendent Dr. Donald Evans on Thursday, August 4, detailing COVID-related guidance for students and parents. The school district is following California Department of Public Health (CDPH) guidelines. “While there are no current indoor masking requirements for schools in California or Alameda County, the wearing of masks in indoor school settings remains strongly recommended,” Dr. Evans said. “All PUSD students and staff are encouraged to wear masks indoors and in any situation where social distancing is limited.” Anyone experiencing symptoms associated with COVID is recommended to wear a mask even after testing negative, he added. Symptoms of COVID include fever, cough, chills, and diarrhea. Students exhibiting such symptoms should “stay at home,” but students who feel “otherwise well enough for school should confirm a negative at-home COVID test before returning to school.” Testing COVID tests are now widely available at pharmacies like Walgreens and CVS, and the City operates a COVID testing clinic near Community Hall five days a week in partnership with health services company Curative. The school district will offer testing as well. Tests will be available at Ellen Driscoll Playhouse, 325 Highland Ave., from 7:45-8:15 a.m. and 8:45-9:15 a.m. on weekdays starting today, August 10 and continuing for at least the first few weeks of the school year. The district can provide a COVID test for home use, as supplies last. A daily health screener for COVID will not be used this academic year. Parents and guests are asked to self-assess before entering campus for symptoms associated with COVID. Tracking cases The school district will continue to track COVID cases in the school community. If your child tests positive, report the absence to their school and complete an online reporting form at http:// Tinyurl.com/pusdgotcovid. Students who test positive should isolate at home for five days, and up to 10 days if symptoms persist. Students testing negative after day five of absence may return to school provided they test negative.
articles.title: Masks at schools strongly recommended but not required

articles.text: Walk for Wellness, an annual fundraiser for Piedmont School District’s Wellness Center, will take place August 21-27 this fall. It is an inclusive series of walks around town and is open to all. The event focuses on physical, mental and emotional wellness. The Wellness Center, on the high school campus, provides confidential, free on-campus and online counseling to all Piedmont High School, Millennium High School and Piedmont Middle School students. The Center also helps students manage common emotional and social challenges of middle and high school including but not limited to stress, depression, grief, family or friendship conflicts, and substance use concerns. articles.text: School starts today, and summer is coming to an end. Your days will soon be filled with soccer and coding classes. But wait – there is one more activity you should consider throwing into the mix. Delivering for the Piedmont Post is a great opportunity for you to do a few things especially if you’re looking for a way to learn independence and reliability. I am one of their paper delivery girls and have to admit something. It’s not all about wearing a newsboy style cap while triumphantly flinging papers that miraculously land on the middle of the door mat. For starters, never fling your papers; no one has that good of an aim. Besides, there is so much more than just delivering papers. You develop life skills and learn personal management with your earnings. I think the best part is talking to all the people you meet along the way. articles.text: Just last week I was delivering papers to a house with a lot of steps. A neighbor came up to me and said, “I know they are on vacation, so let me take it for you.” I remembered this resident because of an interaction around Thanksgiving. He told me that when he was young he used to deliver papers. He then went on to describe how he did it. Apparently, he and a few friends used to stand on a platform on the back of a truck and would fling the papers to the houses. I said that it sounded like fun. “Oh it was,” he replied, “especially Sunday papers.” It’s connections like that that make me smile. One more thing that makes me smile is the memory of one time I was delivering a paper and as soon as I turned around the door opened. The resident called out “Thank you!” It’s the happiness - what people find and see in the paper, and in us, the people delivering the news to them. That’s what I like about delivering papers. articles.text: Get a glimpse of the show at Chabot Space & Science Center this Friday Nothing says summer like a late-night firework show. Mixtures of strontium, calcium, sodium, and many other salts and metal compounds explode into the sky, producing a spectacular array of colors, and then a large BOOM! Fireworks light up the sky in celebrations across the world for Lunar New Year, New Year’s Eve, Bonfire Night, Diwali, and recently the 4th of July. Beyond these special holidays, Mother Nature creates her own beautiful firework displays around 30 times a year — through meteor showers. More about meteors What are meteors? And what are meteor showers? Meteors are small, typically icy rocks that are expelled from comets. When debris from an old comet or asteroid enters the Earth’s atmosphere, a meteor shower occurs. From Earth, we see meteors streak across the sky and leave a fleeting trail of light as they pass by. From July 17-August 24, the Perseid Meteor Shower will take over the sky as the Earth passes through debris from the massive comet, “Swift-Tuttle”. This annual meteor shower is named after the point of the sky where its meteors originate: the Perseus constellation. The Perseid Meteor shower was first observed about 2000 years ago— our ancestors discovered this naturally enchanting light show, and years later, we are still mesmerized by its beauty! Perseid Meteor Shower The Perseid Meteor Shower is the most popular annual shower and it’s easy to see why. Viewers usually can look forward to warm summer temperatures and 50-100 meteors passing by per hour. The best part? The shower can be seen with the naked eye. To get the best views of the celestial event, we recommend being far away from light pollution (streetlamps and other city lights). At Chabot Space & Science Center’s beautiful Observation Deck, which is located in a Redwood forest, our astronomers are hosting a Perseid Meteor Shower Watch Party with hot chocolate to celebrate Mother Nature’s enchanting fireworks. Don’t miss it: this annual shower is considered the best meteor shower of the year by NASA. Come out on the summer evening of August 12th to appreciate the fast and fiery show. Megan Hiller is a Marketing and Communications intern at Chabot Space & Science Center, a non-profit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement and located at 10000 Skyline Blvd. in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth.

ADVERTISE IN THE POST By Megan Hiller Nothing says summer like a late-night firework show. Mixtures of strontium, calcium, sodium, and many other salts and metal compounds explode into the sky, producing a spectacular array of colors, and then a large BOOM! Fireworks light up the sky in celebrations across the world for Lunar New Year, New Year’s Eve, Bonfire Night, Diwali, and recently the 4th of July. Beyond these special holidays, Mother Nature creates her own beautiful firework displays around 30 times a year — through meteor showers. More about meteors What are meteors? And what are meteor showers? Meteors are small, typically icy rocks that are expelled from comets. When debris from an old comet or asteroid enters the Earth’s atmosphere, a meteor shower occurs. From Earth, we see meteors streak across the sky and leave a fleeting trail of light as they pass by. From July 17-August 24, the Perseid Meteor Shower will take over the sky as the Earth passes through debris from the massive comet, “Swift-Tuttle”. This annual meteor shower is named after the point of the sky where its meteors originate: the Perseus constellation. The Perseid Meteor shower was first observed about 2000 years ago— our ancestors discovered this naturally enchanting light show, and years later, we are still mesmerized by its beauty! Perseid Meteor Shower The Perseid Meteor Shower is the most popular annual shower and it’s easy to see why. Viewers usually can look forward to warm summer temperatures and 50-100 meteors passing by per hour. The best part? The shower can be seen with the naked eye. To get the best views of the celestial event, we recommend being far away from light pollution (streetlamps and other city lights). At Chabot Space & Science Center’s beautiful Observation Deck, which is located in a Redwood forest, our astronomers are hosting a Perseid Meteor Shower Watch Party with hot chocolate to celebrate Mother Nature’s enchanting fireworks. Don’t miss it: this annual shower is considered the best meteor shower of the year by NASA. Come out on the summer evening of August 12th to appreciate the fast and fiery show. articles.text: With the new school year starting, Piedmont’s Class of 2023 looks ahead to what could be a defining year of their athletic careers as a senior. articles.text: The Oakland Roots professional soccer team has 10 games left in its season. Currently it is four points back of El Paso Locomotive in seventh place, the final position for possible qualification to the postseason. The Roots currently have six wins, 11 draws, and seven losses with 29 points. “We have 10 Finals to play. For us, every game is important,” said coach Juan Guerra when speaking with the Post. In order to reach the playoffs, Oakland will require some good things to happen. Guerra knows his team will need to win at least five games wins and a draw in the final 10 matches.. “We want to reach 45 points. We believe that’s the mark that will get us into the playoffs. If we keep playing productively, I believe the boys will get us the points we need,” said Guerra. It’s a critical time for Roots supporters to watch scoreboards this week. Monterey Bay faces San Diego Loyal today, August 10. Of note, Monterey is just three games behind Oakland and has played three less matches. On Friday, August 12, third-place Colorado Springs Switchbacks plays El Paso—Oakland will be rooting for a Colorado win. Lastly, last place Orange County hosts ninth-place Phoenix Rising—which holds equal points and one game in hand on Roots. OCSC will need to upset Rising to help out Oakland. The Roots plays this Saturday on the road against Detroit City, its first match since tying 0-0 with Phoenix on July 27. articles.text: The legacy of veteran distance running coach Len Goldman continues. Boys and girls in 4th through 8th grade may sign up for cross-country through what the Recreation Department is calling Piedmont Junior Running Club. It has been offered for many years at the middle school and has proven to be popular as an introduction to running. It will be offered at all elementary schools starting September 12 and will go until the end of October. Practices will be on Mondays and Wednesdays after school. On Mondays, the program will go from 3:15 to 4:30 and on Wednesdays from 2:00 to 3:15. Each session will include not only running, but active games, agility drills, and relay races. All practices will be supervised and directed by adults who are experienced runners and coaches. Middle School X-C team The Piedmont Middle School cross country is coed for all interested students in 6th, 7th and 8th grades. Not in its 17th season, the team practices 4 days a week, Monday through Thursday after school from 3:30 to 5:00 p.m. PMS is in a league with other schools in the East Bay. There will be a series of meets at various parks where students can enjoy friendly competition. Cross-country is a sport any kid can do. There are no plays to learn or athletic skills to master – just running. An experienced coaching staff will lead this program, headed by veteran middle school coaches, Minori Tsuge and Christine Chapon. Sign up for any of the programs being offered by calling the Rec Department at 420-3070, or register on its website: https://piedmont.ca.gov/ activityguide. Adults who would like to help coach are encouraged to contact Akil Danjuma, the Recreation Department’s Sports Coordinator at 420-3089 or by e-mail at adanjuma@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: With the Portola Redwoods State Park announcing this week that it is shutting down its campsites for the remainder of the summer, we return to one of our earlier Hiking With Jon ventures from 2021. When hiking in the park you will see groves of firstand second-generation redwood trees. Portola Redwoods State Park is a 2,800 acre forest, offering a shaded tour through coastal redwoods which are staggeringly larger than those found in the East Bay. The park has 18 miles of hiking trails, although some popular destinations are closed due to COVID-19 protocols – ;ike Tip Toe Falls. Among Portola’s crown jewels is the Old Tree, an estimated 1,200 year old giant at the end of the trail that bears its name: the Old Tree Trail, an easy 1.2 mile out-and-back walk. The Old Tree is 280 feet tall and 12 feet in diameter with burn marks still present on the bark, similar to many other trees found within the park. Aside from the awe-inducing size, the thousandyear-old tree is among the few old growth trees to have survived the mass lumbering of the 1800s. Continuing back to the paved Portola State Park Road, the Summit Trail provides some uphill Staff Photos The Old Big Tree. a redwood tree estimated to be 1,200 years old, 280 feet tall and 12 feet in diameter. Take the Summit Trail to start your loop. The path becomes narrow on the Summit Trail and Slate Creek Trail. Hikers can still see char marks from fires from previous decades along the many first- and second-generation redwoods of Portola State Park. ascent through the hill sides for near two-miles and gaining 550 feet in elevation until intersecting with the Slate Creek Trail. Turn left to start your loop back to your car, intersecting with Peter’s Creek. By turning right, you start a 1.5 mile hike to an historic lumber yard, the Page Mill Site, with the Slate Creek Trail going another two miles and jolting 500 feet in elevation until its end. Portions of the Summit Trail and Slate Creek Trail narrow to a width of less than 6-feet, so you’ll have to be patient when crossing other hikers. If you turned left, the trail continues another 0.8 mile until intersecting with a T. Turning right to make your way to Upper Escape Road, where you turn right again to get a brief glimpse of Peter’s Creek on the trip back to the car – and a pleasant 4-mile day. We passed 40 people on the day, so just 10 people per mile on average. But it’s worth noting that we saw 18 hikers on the 0.6 mile out-and-back Old Tree Trail. Aside from towering redwoods in every direction, you can often spot chickadees chirping about, an occasional banana slug wriggling beneath you, and the knocking of woodpeckers off in the distance. This column was originally printed in the Post in January 2021. You’ll walk along Peter’s Creek on your way back to the car. Watch out for banana slugs, a common sight in coastal parks.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Krcrtv.com Firefighters’ efforts have helped contain the McKinney Fire at 55 percent. The McKinney Fire in the Klamath National Forest near the Oregon border is now at 55 percent containment as of Tuesday, August 9. It was the first time that the blaze experienced no growth since the fire began on July 29. Firefighters were able to construct a line around the fire in an 80-mile perimeter to help extinguishing efforts. “After 11 days of arduous labor, firefighters have accomplished 55 percent containment in the McKinney Fire and have constructed initial line around the entire perimeter. The next step for our fire personnel is to continue to maintain this line by aggressive and thorough mop-up with the intention to gain depth and keep the fire in its existing footprint. Crews continue to patrol and evaluate alternate lines, should the firefighters experience rolling burning material or any spot fires that could challenge their primary line,” wrote Inciweb in a statement, which is a federal fire information site. As of Tuesday, the fire had been burning for 10 days, destroyed 185 structures, damaged another 11, caused 15 injuries, and resulted in four fatalities in Siskiyou County. It is the largest fire this year in California. The fourth reported fatality was longtime U.S. Forest Service employee Kathy Shoopman, who was 73 years old. She died in her home in the Klamath River community as a result of the fire. Siskiyou County was designated as being in extreme drought conditions and is still in red flag conditions. Fire personnel are still keeping a watchful eye on wind and extreme heat. “Anticipate high temperatures, reaching up to 100 degrees, in the Photo courtesy of Yubanet.com The McKinney Fire has caused four fatalities, including 73-year old U.S. Forest Service employee Kathy Shoopman. lower elevations and high 80s in higher elevations. Conditions are expected to be dry with the relative humidity reading 7-8 percent. Winds from the south/southwest could produce gusts up to 35 mph in high elevations. Large dust devils have been observed and are a hazard to look out for on the fire line from the unstable atmosphere. The fire remains in a red flag warning, keeping fire personnel on high alert for any other initial attacks in the area,” wrote Inciweb. Yesterday, August 9, was a critical day in firefighting efforts. It marked the last day of red flag warnings, per California Interagency Incident Management Team fire behavior analyst Dennis Burns. “(Tuesday) is our last day of red flag warnings. If we make it through, I’m starting to feel better that we’re going to keep it, and this fire is going to stay where it belongs,” said Burns. The blaze began on July 29 and rapidly grew in size due due to strong winds and lightning strikes in the area, spreading over 80 square miles in just a two-day span. Conditions have improved greatly since then. Photo courtesy of Wikipedia The McKinney Fire has now burned 60,389 acres, but considerable progress has been made since last week.

Firefighters were able to construct a line around the fire in an 80-mile perimeter to help extinguishing efforts. “After 11 days of arduous labor, firefighters have accomplished 55 percent containment in the McKinney Fire and have constructed initial line around the entire perimeter. Crews continue to patrol and evaluate alternate lines, should the firefighters experience rolling burning material or any spot fires that could challenge their primary line,” wrote Inciweb in a statement, which is a federal fire information site. articles.text: Review by Anastasia Edel Pandemic has made us hermits. Our worlds have shrunk to our families and our phone screens. What was first perceived as a calamity – our home confinements – has become a norm and now, with pandemic easing and medications available, a choice. We spend our weekdays inside our homes on Zoom calls, for which only the upper halves of our bodies need to look presentable, and our weekends roaming the same rooms, backyards, and town blocks, this time without any attempts at presentability. We’ve watched every TV show and hiked every trail. Pandemic is amplifying the affliction of our post-modern world: boredom. Luckily, there are remedies. Going to a live show and watching people perform for other people is one of them. This weekend, San Francisco’s Ballet and Stanford Live teamed up to present “Under the Starry Skies,” a celebration of dance, music, and nature at the Frost Amphitheatre at Stanford University. Judging by the amount of sharply dressed people streaming into the amphitheater – some with their picnic blankets, to sit on the lawn, wine glasses in hand – plenty of us are finally ready to break out of our pandemic shells. That the show was outside made the decision easier. It was good to see the faces of strangers without worrying too much about catching Covid, again. The program’s late start of 8 p.m. gave us ample time to explore Palo Alto’s lively restaurant scene. We had dinner and cocktails at an Indian restaurant so contemporary there was no rice or curries on the menu. Parking at a prepaid Stanford lot was much easier than at the War Memorial Theatre, SF Ballet’s home base – and safer. We didn’t have to worry about our car being vandalized, and no random person screamed at us on our way to the performance. Arriving at our chairs on the Lower Bowl of the grassy amphitheater, a lit-up stage straight ahead, I felt a forgotten sense of excitement. The afternoon breeze had died down. The clouds were gone and a pale half-moon hung above the stage, lantern-style. “Starry nights” offered an eclectic program. It started with Helgi Tomasson’s 7 for Eight, an artistically expressive and technically striking ballet set to four concertos by Johann Sebastian Bach. The precise movements of eight dancers (principal dancer WanTing Zhao was a particular pleasure to watch), Photo by Erik Tomasson Wona Park and Joseph Walsh perform with San Francisco Ballet in William Forsythe’s Blake Works. their strict black costumes, and Bach’s timeless music (occasionally augmented by cicadas in nearby trees), transported the audience. Not a single phone rang or flashed. Without the usual confines of the theatre walls, the stage looked smaller, less formal. When the dancers took their bows to enthusiastic applause, I realized that the daylight was almost entirely gone, and a few pale stars appeared above. Life imitated art. Jerome Robbins’ In the Night moved us some two hundred years forward, from Bach’s baroque and to the romantism of Fredrik Chopin, whose piano etudes provided a musical backdrop for the exploration of relationship stages as portrayed by three different couples. In that piece, passion alternated with reserve, longing with calm, struggle with submission. The dancers were precise and often charming, yet there was less energy, and the narrative drive between the three cameos seemed weak. At times, the couples’ oneby-one performances to a lonely piano score (the orchestra had packed up for the night) had a feel of a high-end recital. But the costumes were marvelous, as was the age-defying Yuan Yuan Tan, a Shanghai-San Francisco miracle, who danced in the final part of the ballet. Because there was no additional rehearsal space, the dancers did their warmups on stage during intermissions. Without shedding one bit of their allure, they looked more approachable during those moments, a bunch of youths in leg warmers, vests, and funny Ugg-style boots you might run into in a school gym. The picture-taking that occurred on stage during intermissions gave another window into the ballet’s enigmatic world, where hours of strenuous practice are alleviated by a sense of camaraderie, and by the plain old fun one must get from effortlessly striking a pose that most of us wouldn’t be able to do even after months of training. The evening concluded with William Forsythe’s Blake Works I, a ballet that, according to San Francisco Chronicle, “explodes your ballet prejudices.” Set to the seven songs of award-winning English musician James Blake’s album The Colour in Anything, the ballet was an innovative exploration of intersections between classical and contemporary. Familiar moves got broken to fit the electronic music (no easy task given that pointe technique requires adherence to certain cannons). Some 30 dancers interpreted songs with lyrics like “Put it Aside and Talk to Me.” Initially rehearsed in pandemic-safe pods, this innovative and vigorous ballet felt like an affirmation of the art – and of the human determination not to give up on it. As the dancers came for their final bows, one couldn’t help but marvel at their physical and mental form, and the effort required to maintain them throughout the long months of lockdowns, quarantines, and masked rehearsals. Those beautiful and talented men and women remain an inspiration, their commitment to the real and the physical piercing the ever-expanding digital bubble. Boredom is simply not in the cards once you put yourself into the genius hands of Helgi Tomassen and his posse. I look forward to the 2023 ballet season with the new artistic director Tamara Rojo. I hope you can join me. Anastasia Edel is a dance, music and art reviewer, and a regular contributor in the New York Times.
articles.title: A summer evening with San Francisco Ballet – at Stanford

articles.text: Rock guitarist Phil Lesh. Stern Grove Festival will close its 85th season with Phil Lesh and Friends this Sunday, August 14. The free concert will include “The Big Picnic,” a benefit for the summer music festival. Lesh, a Berkeley-native, is best known as the bass player for the Grateful Dead for three dcades. He joined his friend Jerry Garcia’s band, the Warlocks, afterward, and remained with the group for its entirety. The Big Picnic is an annual fundraiser benefiting the festival’s mission to present free concerts and provide outreach programs in the Bay Area. The final concert is free and open to the public. Reserved picnic tables for up to 10 people are available for $5,000 - $10,000. For more information on reserving a table, email bigpicnic@ sterngrove.org. Stern Grove Festival Association is a non-profit organization that presents free music festivals in the city since its inception in 1938. articles.text: Paul Walter Hauser protrays the title character, Richard Jewell, in the movie directed by Clint Eastwood. Richard Jewell, a Clint Eastwood film, is based on events that took place during and after the 1996 Atlanta Summer Olympics when a bomb exploded, killing two people and wounding some 100. Working as a security guard that night was Richard Jewell (Paul Walter Hauser), a wannabe police officer, driven by his law and order enthusiasm and his deference to authority. This zealousness has led to the loss of various jobs in law enforcement, from a campus security position to a stint with a local sheriff’s department. Sadly, he seems unable to see himself as others see him, and is puzzled by the ridicule that comes his way – a 33-year-old man, living with his mother, Bobi (Kathy Bates). His core values are pure, and he wishes only to be part of a uniformed cohort that is committed to keeping order. His quest is to find that niche that rewards his sincerity. For him, clearly, police work is more than an identity; it’s a religion and he is its dedicated disciple. The contradiction is that for all of his immersion in policing, he remains an innocent, unable to see the dark side of a world he longs to serve and protect. And so, when the full weight of the F.B.I. and the press/media bear down on him with an unequivocal rush to judgment, he is at best puzzled and is unwilling to believe that he stands accused. He is convinced that no matter the deviousness of the government (they’ve profiled him as a “false hero”) or the rapacious pursuit of headlines by the Atlanta Journal Constitution (AJC), he is insulated by his membership in what he believes to be a fraternity of kindred spirits. His obliviousness is total, despite being interviewed by the Feds and being shown the Journal’s dramatic, accusatory stories. Finally, into this fast moving avalanche of guilt vs. innocence steps a small-time Atlanta attorney, Watson Bryant (Sam Rockwell), who is far from naïve regarding the rights of his new and serendipitously found client. From the get go, Watson attempts, initially without much success, to jolt Richard out of his “cop to cop” compliance, pushing back when he sees his reflexive desire to assist in his own conviction. Slowly, he schools Richard in the facts of the investigation, carried out by a duplicitous agent, Tom Shaw (Jon Hamm), as well as a “whatever it takes” AJC reporter, Kathy Scruggs (Olivia Wilde). And so, Watson steps forward and gives Richard the fierce representation he needs if he has any hope of extracting himself from a profile being etched not only in institutional stone but in public opinion. From the beginning to the end this is a harrowing tale of a man who is the antithesis of anyone remotely close to a “hero bomber,” yet he is just quirky enough and porky enough to make such an identification seem plausible. Having said all that, it should be pointed out that Eastwood has, to a disappointing degree, turned two institutions (the F.B.I. and the press) into caricatures. Both in today’s world are perpetually denigrated by this administration. It gives this film an added chilling relevance. But in the end, this tightly told story is a character study. It is also an example of exceptional actors doing some of their best work. Kathy Bates and Paul Hauser Walker both step fulsomely into their roles and give this fact-based story an abiding verisimilitude. A final note: In the film’s last scene, that takes place some years later, Watson walks into a police station where Richard, in uniform, is standing behind a wide desk, and gives him his long awaited moment of complete redemption. The bomber has been identified. Both nod and smile widely. Finally, at that moment, Richard Jewell’s ordeal has ended. Richard Jewell. Directed by Clint Eastwood. Starring Paul Walter Hauser, Sam Rockwell, Olivia Wilde. Released in 2019 . Now streaming on VUDU/Prime? Apple tv. 2hrs 9min. Rated R.

articles.text: Horton Hears a Who! is an animated feature based on the popular Dr. Seuss children’s book. It was released into theaters in 2008 and is now streaming. The story begins with a wisp of dust, a mere speck, floating through the jungle of Nool. This dot on a clover is actually a self-contained planet that exits in its own cosmos. Along comes Horton (Jim Carrey), a gentle pachyderm who believes that an elephant is “faithful one hundred percent.” Of course, with his large ears, to his surprise, he hears a voice coming from the tiny dust moat. Following the tiny alarmed voice, Horton discovers that it’s coming from a microcosmic city called Who-ville, and the call for help is coming from Who-ville’s daffy mayor Ned McDodd (Steve Carrell). The call for help by the mayor is caused by his belief that Whoville is in serious danger. Horton agrees to help, believing that a “person is a person, no matter how small,” and agrees to move Who-ville to a safer sanctuary. When Horton tells some of the denizens of the jungle of Nool about the existence of Who-ville, they laugh and ridicule him, as does the Kangaroo (Carol Channing), who is snootily derisive. Even Horton’s best friend, Morton the mouse (Seth Rogen), doesn’t believe that there could be such a place as Who-ville. And the citizens of Who-ville doubt the mayor. “What peril?” they ask, even when it begins to snow during the summer. But one person believes Ned, and that’s Dr. Larue, a purple-haired nerdette (Isla Fisher) with thick safety glasses, who supports the mayor and believes that the city should be moved to the top of Mt. Nool where they will not be in peril. It’s a given that Horton Hears a Who! will connect with younger kids and plays to their curiosity. And not to forget that there’s a bevy of creatures that will appeal, such as a goofy vulture named Vlad (Will Arnett), and Tommy, a fat orange bear (Jonar Nila). And not to forget that there are, of course, some gentle life lessons about friendship that never come off as lectures. It’s all lots of fun, quirky, and good natured. Horton Hears a Who! Animated adventure- comedy. Directed by Jimmy Hayward and Steve Marino. With voices of Jim Carrey, Steve Carrell, Amy Poehler, and Isla Fisher. 1 hr., 28 min. Rated G. Released in 2008. articles.text: On July 18, seven Scouts from Troop 15 and three adults set out on the Troop’s annual Sierra trek for four days and three nights of backpacking near beautiful South Lake Tahoe. The trip followed 25 miles on the Pacific Crest Trail and Tahoe Rim Trail. pages.text: Wednesday, August 10, 2022 23 Defining creativity My family, in all their creative individuality. By Laura Martin Bovard As a parent, I have to frequently check that I am not labeling our children. I’ve noticed it only serves to make them question their uniqueness. What seemed like a harmless way of acknowledging what is special about them I realize can devolve into labels and comparisons that unintentionally make them feel bad about themselves. Once Scott and I saw the error of our ways, we really tried to put the kibosh on that behavior. Still, we aren’t perfect. Every once in a while, I’ll catch myself comparing them, and have to remember not to. I have often said that growing my business has taught me to be a more self-aware, conscious person, and that is even more true when it comes to raising children. Like my business, I don’t think I grew them as much as they grew me. I imagine that most of us bear the wounds of being labeled when we were children either by our parents, our teachers, or other well-meaning elders. One of the labels my own father frequently repeated was that my brother Steve was “the creative one.” It didn’t occur to me to be offended or disagree with that statement at the time. He was my father – the boss, and the holder of all knowledge. It made sense to me at the age of 8 to believe him, so I did. What he meant was that Steve could draw well, which was true. Because he had an interest in it, he drew and drew and got better and better. One could surmise that yes, in fact, Steve was a creative one. But it turns out he wasn’t the creative one. He was simply creative. Meanwhile, during the era Steve received his honorary title, I was the one making leis, selling lemonade, cooking up a storm in the kitchen, and decorating and redecorating every room in the house. I also loved to tutor my younger siblings so they could get a leg up in school and be well prepared. I adored my English classes and wrote regularly in my journal. I was constantly curious. Being the patriarchal guy that he was, my father characterized my kind of creativity as “women’s work,” which was expected rather than celebrated. Women’s work came second to that of boys and men, and so I did not reap the same status for my efforts as my brother did. It may seem blatantly obvious to anyone who knows me that I am a creative person. I design, I write, I am an entrepreneur, and I curate life in general. But because of the labels that were placed on me that I accepted hook, line, and sinker, it’s taken me a long time to actually own the fact that I am creative. I used the output of my creative energy to serve others. Now that I’ve shifted my thinking and allowed that truth to be my own, I am enjoying my life infinitely more. I invite anyone who rejects the idea that they are creative to challenge that thought. We are creating our lives in every moment of every day. Creativity isn’t just painting, drawing, or playing the piano. It’s also how we put ourselves together, how we present ourselves to the world. We create every time we choose our words, get dressed, and make a meal. If we slow down and approach these daily practices as an art form instead of rushing through to the finish line, all these things can be considered creative. It’s in the how. So next time, before you utter the words “I’m not creative,” slow down and ask yourself if that’s really true. It’s all in how you define it. articles.text: A road rage altercation over a traffic maneuver early morning on August 2 on Oakland Avenue turned violent when six shots were fired and two struck the victim’s car. The victim, an Oakland resident in an Acura LX, was driving on Oakland Avenue near Monte Vista at around 6:30 a.m. when suspects behind him in a newer white Alfa-Romeo took offense to a traffic maneuver and honked their horn. The driver of the Acura honked back and some words were exchanged. “It got a little crazy after that,” said Piedmont Police Captain Chris Monahan. Six shots were fired from the Alfa-Romeo near Oakland Avenue and Olive Avenue in Piedmont, hence the jurisdiction fell to Piedmont Police. Two of the bullets struck the Acura. One went through the trunk, and then through the backseat, before stopping in the headrest on the driver side. The other bullet entered the victim’s Acura above the taillight and ricocheted around in the frame. Four other shots were fired but have not been located. No bullet shell casings were found. Crime lab analysis is being done on the bullet found lodged in the back of the headrest. The driver was not injured. “We’ve got some video from a homeowner where you can hear the shots and see the victim vehicle, but we never see the suspect vehicle in the video,” said Monahan. No images of the suspect vehicle have yet to be collected, but based on the victim’s descriptions, police estimate it to be a 2015-2020 white fourdoor Alfa-Romeo with paper plates and “dark rims.” The model is rare in the United States. The victim said there were at least three people in the Alfa-Romeo, and one of them fired a handgun. The car was going approximately 45 miles per hour when the shots were fired. Once the victim saw the suspects were no longer behind him, he pulled onto Sunnyside Avenue to collect himself. He then continued to drive to work and called 911 later from his office in Oakland. The Piedmont Police Department is actively investigating this crime, in conjunction with other local agencies. “Our detectives have been inspecting matching vehicles stopped by other law enforcement agencies. That will continue until we find the suspect vehicle,” Monahan said. Anyone with information associated to this event, including surveillance images from the area, are asked to contact Det, George Tucker at (510) 420-3013 or Det. John Lagios at (510) 420- 3015. pages.text: Wednesday, August 10, 2022 29 CRIME REPORT Bullets fired in August 2 road rage incident By Jay Russell A road rage altercation over a traffic maneuver early morning on August 2 on Oakland Avenue turned violent when six shots were fired and two struck the victim’s car. The victim, an Oakland resident in an Acura LX, was driving on Oakland Avenue near Monte Vista at around 6:30 a.m. when suspects behind him in a newer white Alfa-Romeo took offense to a traffic maneuver and honked their horn. The driver of the Acura honked back and some words were exchanged. “It got a little crazy after that,” said Piedmont Police Captain Chris Monahan. Six shots were fired from the Alfa-Romeo near Oakland Avenue and Olive Avenue in Piedmont, hence the jurisdiction fell to Piedmont Police. Two of the bullets struck the Acura. One went through the trunk, and then through the backseat, before stopping in the headrest on the driver side. The other bullet entered the victim’s Acura above the taillight and ricocheted around in the frame. Four other shots were fired but have not been located. No bullet shell casings were found. Crime lab analysis is being done on the bullet found lodged in the back of the headrest. The driver was not injured. “We’ve got some video from a homeowner where you can hear the shots and see the victim vehicle, but we never see the suspect vehicle in the video,” said Monahan. No images of the suspect vehicle have yet to be collected, but based on the victim’s descriptions, police estimate it to be a 2015-2020 white fourdoor Alfa-Romeo with paper plates and “dark rims.” The model is rare in the United States. The victim said there were at least three people in the Alfa-Romeo, and one of them fired a handgun. The car was going approximately 45 miles per hour when the shots were fired. Once the victim saw the suspects were no longer behind him, he pulled onto Sunnyside Avenue to collect himself. He then continued to drive to work and called 911 later from his office in Oakland. The Piedmont Police Department is actively investigating this crime, in conjunction with other local agencies. “Our detectives have been inspecting matching vehicles stopped by other law enforcement agencies. That will continue until we find the suspect vehicle,” Monahan said. Anyone with information associated to this event, including surveillance images from the area, are asked to contact Det, George Tucker at (510) 420-3013 or Det. John Lagios at (510) 420- 3015. If this vehicle is seen, call 911 immediately and reference the event. pages.text: 32 Wednesday, August 10, 2022 Northern Teir Continued from page 24 serving as a guide to help the Scouts organize and plan their routes. The first morning the Scouts picked up their food, checked out their canoes and learned how to lift their canoe onto their shoulders. By 10 a.m. each crew was launched and heading out. Scouts rotated camp duties during the trip, including cooking, cleaning, setting up the rain fly, and hanging a bear bag with a food box. The Scouts also performed conservation projects, cleaning at each campsite they visited, picking up any trash left over from prior visitors. Crew Leaders Ethan and Kai chose adventurous routes with a goal of paddling a total of 50 miles. Both crews met their paddling goals. Both crews went east due to routes in the west being flooded, with water levels up nearly 5 feet making it difficult to find and navigate portages. Ethan´s crew was filled with Members of Crew #2: William Campbell (left), Miguel Long, Alex Cantrill, Nico Jerez, Kai Lambert, Javier Jerez, and Jason Lambert. nearly all anglers, who caught fresh fish nearly every night, providing the Scouts with dinners of bass, Northern pike, and lake trout. Liam´s crew was focused more on the beautiful waters. They turned a bad weather day into a night to remember as they woke up at 4 a.m. and did a 14-mile night paddle on the moonlit lakes. Miguel Long caught the majority of the fish for Kai´s crew while the group took a day trip in order to explore a beautiful waterfall. Ethan´s crew had an epic fishing experience with Henry Smith catching the biggest fish of the trip, a huge 5+ pound smallmouth bass on a fly rod. During the week, Ethan´s crew caught more than 80 nice fish. Both crews crossed many lakes and had almost 12 portages, hiking with all their gear, camping equipment, while carrying 16-foot canoes on their shoulders. At least one adult leader from each crew was well trained in CPR and first aid. The Scouts experienced thunderstorms and beautiful lightning strikes as well as waters too windy and rough to travel on. Aside from the mosquitos, Scouts saw a bobcat, moose, beavers, loons, rabbits, and even turtles. Both crews earned the 50-miler award, which is given to crews who paddle 50 miles in around 5 days. For everyone, it was the trip of a lifetime! Ethan Alering is a sophomore at Piedmont High School and a member of Piedmont Scout Troop 11.
